newsitem.title: FRANCE: Bernard Kouchner, France's humanitarian Action Man.
newsitem.headline: Bernard Kouchner, France's humanitarian Action Man.

text.p: Bernard Kouchner, the outspoken founder of the medical aid charity Medecins Sans Frontieres and a champion of humanitarian intervention, was named secretary of state for health in France's Socialist-led cabinet on Wednesday.
Kouchner, a 57-year-old whose good looks and combative manner made him a media star, arouses both antipathy for publicity-seeking and admiration as an advocate of refugees and war victims.

As humanitarian action minister from 1988 to 1993, he helped to persuade the United Nations to intervene in the affairs of another country for the first time by setting up a protection zone for the Kurds of northern Iraq after the 1991 Gulf War.
"National sovereignty does not give you the right to massacre your own people," he says.

But Kouchner's comeback into government came as a surprise. After failing to find a constituency for the National Assembly elections, he said in February that he was quitting politics and leaving for Sudan to open a hospital. "My friends have stabbed me in the back," he complained.
He never left. Instead, he became one of Socialist leader Lionel Jospin's "seven musketeers" who fanned out across France during the campaign to attract leftist votes.

Kouchner was the man behind the "French doctors," the aid workers who, from the late 1960s, broke the rules of diplomatic etiquette by taking relief to war victims without first asking permission from the strongmen responsible for their misery.

But his hair-trigger enthusiasm and blunt speaking did not always endear him to his cabinet colleagues. When famine and civil war in Somalia peaked in December 1992, he personally carried a bag of rice into Mogadishu.

The gesture before a clutch of television crews caused a furore back home, where a critical press denounced it as self-promotion in a country where the problem was not lack of food but inability to prevent armed gangs stealing it.
Kouchner was pugnaciously unrepentant. "Who disapproved of me?" he thundered. "Certainly not the Somali children."

The moment was classic Kouchner: although the United Nations had been on the ground for several months, he made it look to his home audience as if he had upstaged the rest of the world community. The U.N.-mandated Operation Restore Hope began a few days later.
After the Somalia episode some maliciously nicknamed him "Uncle Ben" after the American brand of rice.

Kouchner came to personify a mixture of personal idealism and media awareness in 25 years of relief work: from Biafra in the mid-1960s and in Jordan among Palestinian refugees to Kurdistan, Sudan, Ethiopia, Armenia and Yugoslavia.
Kouchner was born in Avignon on September 1, 1939, the day Germany invaded Poland at the outset of World War Two.
As a medical student and then as a young gastro-enterologist he flirted with the far left, but spent the turbulent days of May 1968 far from riot-torn Paris in Biafra for the Red Cross.
Outraged at the Red Cross's reluctance to intervene to help civilian victims, Kouchner set up Medecins sans Frontieres and, a decade later, its sister organisation Medecins du Monde.
